newsitem.title: UK: Dollar sturdy in Europe as soft-euro talk swells.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sturdy in Europe as soft-euro talk swells.

text.p: Dollar/mark was lodged near previous European closing levels in early trade here, supported by fears France's left-wing election victors would pave the way for a broad-based, soft single currency.
French Socialist Elisabeth Guigou, tipped for office in Lionel Jospin's new government, said her party would respect the 1999 start date for European economic and monetary union.

Traders said this fuelled the belief gaining currency in the market -- that France's political swing would mean a timely but soft euro, rather than the more mark-supportive scenario of EMU delay. That, they said, was good news for the dollar.

"We know the Socialists want to go ahead on time, but we know they're not so committed to actually meeting the criteria themselves -- that's underpinning the dollar," said Thomas Rayner, international economist at SGST.

With the Socialists opposed to further austerity measures, pushing for Italy and Spain in EMU from the start and suggesting renegotiating the stability pact, analysts saw plenty to feed fears of a soft euro.
The ongoing row between the Bundesbank and Bonn over German government plans to revalue assets to help qualify for EMU has been overshadowed but can only stoke those fears, they said.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7283/86 marks at 0807 GMT, up from late Monday's European level of 1.7265/75 though off overnight highs around 1.7330.
Dollar/yen edged down to 116.12/22 from its previous close here of 116.55/65.
A rumour that influential Japanese finance ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said the yen may firm to 103 per dollar unsettled the dollar/yen overnight. But traders were secptical.
"They've got (the yen) more or less where they want it now. Why rock the boat by making statements?" said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe in London.

Analysts saw little scope for the dollar to extend Monday's gains much on Tuesday, barring fresh shocks out of Europe, but said any firm U.S. data out later this week could propel the dollar through its 1997 peak of 1.7389 marks.
A stronger than expected National Association of Purchasing Managers' Index for May released yesterday painted a rosy picture of the U.S. economy, showing new orders strong but inflation subdued.
The only U.S. data due out today are April leading indicators at 1400 GMT, and the market is now keenly awaiting May non-farm payrolls figures, to be released on Friday.

A strong figure will fuel expectations of U.S. tightening at the next Federal Reserve policy-making meeting in July. Many economists have drastically lowered their forecasts, however, after seasonal revisions by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Economists polled by Reuters expect payrolls to have risen by 221,000 on average after increasing 142,000 in April.

Sterling remained supported as the market sought out havens from European turmoil. It was quoted at 2.8220/30 marks at 0828 GMT versus late yesterday's 2.8225/35, with cable at $1.6326/36 compared to $1.6345/55.
Elsewhere, the market awaited a news conference in Sweden at 1430 GMT, at which the government will deliver its view on Swedish participation in European monetary union.
Economists expect a qualified "no" to EMU membership, ruling out participation from the start in January 1999 but leaving the door open for participation later if public opposition wanes.

In Finland, dealers said the central bank had sold markka for marks at around 3.0050 in a bid to prevent its currency from strengthening further. The markka stood at 3.0040/70 per mark at 0838 GMT versus late Monday's 3.0090/120.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
